newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia PM fails to convince farmers on land deal.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM fails to convince farmers on land deal.

text.p: Thousands of angry Australian farmers on Saturday overwhelmingly rejected Prime Minister John Howard's proposed land claims solution, saying it failed to give them the security they have demanded.
Howard was outlining the details of his 10-point native title plan to a meeting of about 2,000 farmers from all over Australia in the outback town of Longreach in the northern Queensland state.
He told farmers his plan guaranteed that no pastoral leaseholder could lose land or could be stopped from carrying on business as a result of native title claims.
"(Under my plan) no pastoral titleholder can have their title in any way affected or diminished," he said.

"But most importantly of all, you can go away from this meeting safe in the knowledge that when this legislation is passed in the national parliament, you will have the full and unfettered capacity to run your property."
Howard's plan guarantees farmers' rights to land they have leased since European settlement began more than 200 years ago, while also allowing Aborigines limited access for traditional purposes.
But the farmers have said the compromise deal does not provide them with the certainty they need to successfully continue their business.
Aborigines have also criticised the plan, saying it effectively wipes out native title and sets their rights back 50 years.

Native title laws were introduced by the former Labor government three years ago, but became an urgent political issue when the High Court decided last December that land leased to farmers could be liable to Aboriginal claim.
Despite Howard's promises, the overwhelming majority of farmers at the meeting later voted in favour of blanket extinguishing of native title.
"The message was very clearly that they weren't convinced," United Graziers Association president Larry Acton said after the meeting which included 2-1/2 hours of questions.
Up to 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles) could be affected by native title claims.
